Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

</document>
response:
I've read it closely. I checked the arithmetic first: the per-sector conversions, the employee-weighted mean (98.73), the totals (61 organisations, 2,940 staff) and the secondary-outcome percentages all reproduce correctly. The problems are in the interpretation. The headline claims, especially "sector-general," don't follow from the data, and some of the paper's own numbers point the other way.

## 1. The output-per-hour gain is largely mechanical

Output per scheduled hour is the output index divided by 0.8. Any organisation whose output fell by less than 20% therefore shows a gain, and an unchanged output shows +25%.

- "Gains in output per hour in every sector" was all but guaranteed by construction. It is not an independent finding.
- The Limitations section says the result is unlikely to be overturned "given its size and consistency across sectors." But the size and the consistency are both properties of the formula, not evidence of robustness.
- The informative quantity is the output index itself, and on that measure the pilot's own principle ("100% of the output") was not met overall (98.7). In retail and hospitality it was clearly not met (93.1).

## 2. The retail evidence contradicts the "sector-general" conclusion

- **Output fell.** Retail output dropped 6.9%, the only sector with a material fall. The paper describes this as "close to baseline" and recasts it as a +16.4% productivity gain.
- **Half the retail organisations reverted.** Three of the five reversions were in retail, out of only six retail organisations. Two more were in healthcare administration, out of five. Pooling these into a "92% continuation" figure hides that 50% and 40% of the two customer-facing sectors abandoned the schedule.
- **Coverage costs are unreported.** Seventeen organisations used staggered days off to maintain coverage. In shift-based sectors, coverage often needs extra staff or overtime, but headcount changes and total paid hours aren't reported. Output per *employee's* scheduled hour can rise while output per *organisation* labour hour, or per unit of wage cost, falls.
- **Unit labour costs rose.** With pay unchanged and output at 98.7, labour cost per unit of output rose about 1.3% overall and about 7.4% in retail. That is the number an employer would weigh.

The data are consistent with the opposite of the paper's claim: reduced hours worked roughly in knowledge-work sectors and were strained in customer-facing ones. Self-selection makes this worse. The retail organisations that volunteered were presumably the most suited to the model, and half still reverted.

## 3. The primary outcome is weak

- **Rated by interested parties.** The output index was completed by managers who were responsible for the pilot's success.
- **No common definition.** It used "whatever output records the organisation held," with no shared metric, no validation and no audit.
- **No precision reported.** The paper gives no confidence intervals, no organisation-level distribution and no variance. Sector means rest on five to nineteen organisations.
- **Scheduled versus actual hours.** Limitation 4 concedes that actual hours may have fallen by less than 20%. If staff absorbed part of the cut through longer days or work on the day off, the true per-hour gain could be far smaller, and the paper has no way to bound it.

Given all this, the 23.4% figure carries far more precision than the measurement supports.

## 4. The revenue evidence is weaker than presented

- **Nominal, not real.** The 1.4% rise is presumably nominal. Pilot timing (recruitment in early 2023 plus two months' preparation) puts it in a period of roughly 4–7% inflation in many economies, so real revenue likely fell. "No sign that output was sacrificed" doesn't hold. It is at least a possible sign.
- **Different baseline.** Revenue is compared with the previous year, while output is compared with the preceding six months, so the two aren't directly comparable.
- **Possible selective reporting.** Nine organisations didn't report revenue. If they were disproportionately the weaker performers, the figure is biased upward.

## 5. The secondary outcomes need adjustment

- **Sick days are partly mechanical.** With 20% fewer scheduled days, there are 20% fewer days on which to be absent. The mechanical expectation is about 4.4 × 0.8 ≈ 3.5. The genuine reduction is therefore roughly 2.8 versus 3.5, about −20%, not −36%. It may be lower still if the baseline window and pilot window differ seasonally, since six-month figures are annualised and the baseline season isn't stated.
- **Resignations have other explanations.** A large fall in resignations is plausible and valuable, but it may reflect employees not wanting to leave a four-day job rather than reduced fatigue. With no control group, it is also confounded with the 2023 cooling of labour markets.
- **Energy decayed between surveys.** Self-reported energy rose 0.61 SD at month three but only 0.29 SD at month six. That is a halving in three months, consistent with novelty or Hawthorne effects, and it is the main warning in the data about longer-run effects. The Discussion doesn't mention it.
- **Survey details are missing.** Response rates and attrition between survey waves aren't reported. Self-rated productivity ("64% higher than before") from staff who benefit from the policy is weak evidence.

## 6. The causal story isn't supported

- **Fatigue versus process change.** The Discussion names reduced fatigue as "the most plausible single explanation." The paper's own interview evidence points equally to process changes: fewer meetings (47 of 58 managers), focus blocks and dropped reporting. Several managers called the pilot a "forcing device."
- **Different policy implications.** If process changes did the work, they might be achievable without cutting hours. The design can't distinguish the two explanations, so neither should be favoured.
- **Continuation is weak evidence.** Reverting is costly, since staff would resist. The decision-makers were self-selected champions of the pilot, and the 92% conceals the sector split described above.

## 7. The summary overstates the conclusion

The Conclusion is relatively measured: "compatible with near-unchanged output," and further pilots should include a comparison group. The Summary and Discussion go further: "sector-general," "no basis for the common view." The limitations listed (self-selection, no control, manager-rated output, scheduled hours) each bear directly on that stronger claim, but the paper sets them aside rather than letting them qualify it.

## What the data do support

Among self-selected, mostly knowledge-work organisations, a 20% cut in scheduled hours was associated with manager-reported output close to baseline. It was also associated with lower sickness absence (after adjusting for fewer scheduled days), substantially lower resignations and lower reported burnout. Effects on energy faded during the pilot. In retail and healthcare administration, output fell more and reversions were common.

## Suggested revisions

1. Lead with the output index rather than output per scheduled hour, and state that the per-hour figure is mechanical.
2. Report organisation-level distributions and confidence intervals, plus headcount and total paid hours by sector.
3. Report revenue in real terms, and say which organisations didn't report it.
4. Express sick days per scheduled day, and state the baseline window.
5. Report reversion rates by sector, and remove the "sector-general" claim.
6. Discuss the decline in energy between month three and month six.
7. Present fatigue and process change as competing explanations the design can't separate.
8. Collect actual hours worked from at least a subsample.

I can draft a revised Summary and Discussion along these lines if that would help.
